https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/pride-org.text: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent Updated Thu, 23 July 2026 at 9:27 am UTC 0 Organisers submitted more than 100 proposed routes to authorities in Oradea, but all were rejectedPhotograph: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Campaigners in a Romanian city have vowed to go ahead with a Pride march after local authorities denied permission for the fourth consecutive year. Since 2023, campaigners in the western city of Oradea, which has a population of about 180,000, have sought permission to hold Pride events. However, each year they have faced opposition, making Oradea the only major city in the EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride marches. “Every year the local authorities have managed to find legal or technical excuses to ban Oradea Pride events,” said Iulian Dițiu, the co-founder and president of Ark Oradea, the local organiser of Pride. In 2024, they were told none of the city’s parks were available at the times requested, he said. The following year, campaigners submitted 12 potential routes for the march, only to be told that none was suitable. In the run-up to Saturday’s proposed march, organisers submitted more than 100 possible routes. On Wednesday, the city authorities said none of them was viable because they clashed with other events or public infrastructure works. The mayor, who belongs to a party that describes itself as liberal, conservative and Christian democratic, did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Dițiu said the repeated refusals sent a broader message. “It feels like the message that they are trying to send our way is that we’re not welcome here,” he said. “They have never said out loud that they are banning Pride for LGBT reasons. They’re always hiding behind technical reasons.” The dispute has attracted growing international attention. More than 152 organisations from 30 countries have signed a statement calling on officials to allow the march to take place “in complete safety” and in line with EU law. “After four consecutive years in which the Pride march has been unable to take place, there can be no question of administrative or logistical difficulties,” the statement said. “When an authority consistently prevents a community from assembling peacefully, a principle that concerns all citizens is undermined.” Their appeal, delivered recently to the local administration in Oradea, drew comparisons between Oradea and Budapest, where Hungary’s former prime minister Viktor Orbán and his rightwing populist movement had sought to ban Pride events. “In recent years, the restriction of Pride marches has become, in several European states, an indicator of democratic backsliding and the weakening of the rule of law,” the statement said. Dițiu said organisers intended to proceed with the march on Saturday despite the lack of official permission, repeating last year’s approach. In 2025, between 500 and 600 people attended an unauthorised march, with nine participants later fined the equivalent of about €4,000 (£3,420) he said. This time representatives from several diplomatic missions have said they will take part, along with Romania’s ombudsman, he added. Dițiu described the situation as both “encouraging and disappointing”. “The institutions that are supposed to protect the rights of every community are trying to use our community as a scapegoat. But many more people are behind us. Many more people understand what the stakes are,” he said. “This is not an LGBT issue. This is a democratic issue. It’s about the freedom to public assembly. And if the local LGBT community here in Oradea can be denied this basic human right without any repercussion, it can happen pretty much anywhere in Europe, for pretty much any community.” Show comments 0 Advertisement From Our Partners Advertisement Advertisement Business Live Admiral profit falls 18% as UK car insurance division reports decline Express UK Barclays warning over customer account change ahead of August deadline Express UK Shopkeeper dies after alleged bashing by gang of children as young as 12 Express UK Gianni Infantino threatens to move World Cup final venue in drastic crisis meeting mo… Express UK Met Office gives verdict on next UK heatwave as weather maps turn red for 34C scorche… The Guardian New Zealand capital delights in rare snowfall as southern city residents ski down wor… Advertisement Contact Feedback Help Cookie Policy EU Digital Services Act Terms and Privacy Policy Privacy Dashboard About Our Ads About Us Sitemap

RRI Encyclopedia Steliu Lambru , 20.09.2026, 14:00 The most spectacular section of the Danube, along its 2,850-kilometer course from the Black Forest Mountains in Germany to its mouth on the Black Sea in Romania, is its gorge. There, the great river cuts through the Carpathian Mountains and offers the world a unique natural habitat. However, as spectacular as the landscape is there, navigation was just as dangerous until the mid-19 th century. Historical sources record shipwrecks, sinking, and groundings, with the Cazane (Cauldrons) section being the most difficult part of the gorge for navigation. Major projects almost always enjoy political backing. Following the peace treaties that concluded the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, the Austro-Hungarian administration undertook a project to facilitate navigation on the Danube. Consequently, a canal over two kilometers long, 73 meters wide, and four meters deep was excavated along the right bank of the river. It began opposite the town of Orșova and ended near the village of Sip, taking the village’s name. In 1969, 73 years after its inauguration, the construction of the Iron Gates hydroelectric dam caused the water level in the reservoir to rise, submerging the Sip Canal. Engineer Michael Românu is a postcard collector who has gathered photographs of the Danube Gorge area over the years. He has restored items that were dirty, torn, yellowed, or missing parts. He has organized exhibitions featuring Băile Herculane, Old Orșova, the Danube Gorge, Turnu Severin, the Danube’s Iron Gates or Cauldrons (Cazanele), the Reșița Steam Locomotive Factory, and Ada Kaleh Island. To mark the 130 th anniversary of the opening of the Sip Canal, Michael Românu curated an exhibition displaying 240 photographs and postcards in 10×15 cm and A4 formats: “130 years passed since the inauguration of the Sip Canal, which played an extraordinarily important role, not only for Romania and its future but also for all of Central Europe and beyond. I say this because the stretch of the Danube between Turnu Severin and Baziaș was riddled with rapids. It was an area filled with submerged rocks that had to be removed to make navigation at least somewhat feasible for river vessels, cargo barges, and other craft.” Michael Românu believes we must always remember our predecessors, those who created the images that form today’s archives. One such figure was the photographer Geza Hutterer (1864–1917): “I dedicate all my exhibitions to a photographer named Geza Hutterer. He lived in Orșova and, throughout his life, from 1890 to 1917, took a vast number of photographs in this area. Thanks to him, we now have the wonderful opportunity to see what life was like back then, and what the people, places, and towns looked like.” We asked Michael Românu to describe the exhibition in which he presents a lost project to the eyes of the modern viewer. He explained: “The 240 photographs form a novel, by analogy; all my photographs are organized into chapters. The exhibition on the Sip Canal begins with the first chapter, showing the rock formations that once existed in the Danube’s riverbed. Next come the machinery and river vessels used to construct the Sip Canal. Another chapter follows, depicting scenes from the actual construction work. Then comes the inauguration of the Sip Canal. In this section, I have several photographs that play a crucial role, as they document events from September 26 th , the day before the official opening, when Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria-Hungary arrived at the Orșova railway station and met King Carol I of Romania. King Aleksandar of Serbia also arrived there. Together, they went into the town of Orșova and visited the old town. Afterward, they attended a brief religious service at the Catholic church in Orșova. From there, they traveled together to Băile Herculane spa resort. It is well known that Băile Herculane was an exceptionally important resort at the time; even Empress Sisi of Austria visited annually. After concluding their visit to Orșova and Băile Herculane, they departed together from the Orșova commercial port aboard the passenger steamer ‘Franz Joseph’, heading for the Sip Canal. Upon arrival, they docked at a pontoon and were greeted by thousands of people who had gathered for the canal’s inauguration. From there, they traveled to Bucharest and, subsequently, to Sinaia. The construction of the Sip Canal enabled barges laden with crude oil to reach Orșova, where the oil was unloaded into two large reservoirs at the commercial port. It was then pumped into railway tank cars and transported from there, over a distance of 2.5 to 3 kilometers, to the refinery, or the Orșova Oil Factory, as it was known at the time.” 130 years ago, the Sip Canal opened, a true breakthrough for pan-European Danube navigation. Today, however, it exists only as a memory, one that, fortunately, has also been preserved in images. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/russ.text: Russia dismissed calls for transparency over the death of a laboratory technician from plague in Siberia on Wednesday, as reports emerged of a second case of infection.Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said it saw "no epidemic risk" following the death of a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, identified as Darya Shipilova, who died last week in the town of Shelekhov near Irkutsk.The agency said Shipilova had been "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with," and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.More than 90% of those who had contact with her had completed medical monitoring, it said.The Kremlin dismissed reports of a second suspected plague case in Siberia, telling journalists that most media reporting on the situation was "false"."The media are reporting a great deal right now, and the overwhelming majority of what the media are reporting around this situation is false information," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, urging citizens to rely solely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements.Russian authorities have maintained since the start of the week that Shipilova died of pneumonia and that her cause of death remains "undetermined".International concern persistsUS President Donald Trump had a call with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin scheduled for Wednesday to address the plague incident, and his administration sent Moscow a demarche requesting additional information."We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said on Wednesday.Peskov said he had no information that the Kremlin had received any US official complaint.WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus on Wednesday called on Moscow to clarify the situation over media reports of a second staff member with pneumonia of unclear origin."Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing in line with the International Health Regulations is critical," Tedros said.The WHO said the day before that the possible case posed a "very low" risk beyond Russia's borders, citing the country's reduced contact with the rest of the world due to its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and resulting sanctions.It noted that the institute studied "dangerous pathogens" and that plague occurs naturally among wild animals in the Irkutsk region.Pneumonic plague, the most dangerous form of the disease, affects the lungs and can spread person to person through airborne droplets, with an incubation period as short as 24 hours.It can be fatal without appropriate care, but the chances of recovery are high if identified and treated promptly. Symptoms include shortness of breath, coughing and blood-streaked sputum.The more common bubonic plague is caused by the bite of an infected flea and can produce purulent ulcers.If verified, the Siberia case would be Russia's first confirmed plague infection since 2016.

https://www.prokerala.com/news/articles/.text: Atlanta, Oct 31 : Poland has secured India's support for its bid to become a permanent G20 member and hopes to join during the US presidency, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said. Responding to a question from IANS at a press conference, Sikorski said the United States had tabled a resolution proposing permanent membership for Poland. He said he had been lobbying colleagues to support the move and had sought India's backing. Prime Minister Narendra Modi had committed India's backing while receiving Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in India a few days earlier, Sikorski said. "We are grateful for that." Asked how long the membership process would take, he replied: "That depends. We hope it'll happen during the American presidency." Sikorski referred to the forthcoming summit in Florida. He also said Britain had already invited Tusk to attend next year in Manchester. "But as I've mentioned already, the British presidency has already invited us as well." He did not give a firm date for a decision on Poland's application. Sikorski said his campaign for support included discussions with counterparts from Argentina, Canada, Korea and Indonesia. He had also held discussions with Saudi Arabia, with a formal bilateral meeting planned for the following day. He said almost all the counterparts he had approached had agreed to support Poland's membership. "Some have already declared it publicly." On relations with India, Sikorski described Tusk's visit as "extremely successful". The Polish leader had travelled with ministers responsible for areas offering scope for cooperation, alongside dozens of businesspeople, he said. Sikorski also welcomed the prospect of an India-European Union free trade agreement. He said developments had accelerated and expressed hope that the agreement would benefit both sides. He noted that some people in Poland had been sceptical about the EU-Mercosur agreement, but said the initial figures were encouraging. He expressed similar hopes for mutual benefits from an agreement with India. Sikorski also referred to an Indian initiative when asked about efforts to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea. "Well, there is the Turkish initiative; as you know, there is the Indian initiative." He urged quick action, citing the needs of people in the Global South. He did not provide details of the Indian initiative. Asked whether he had held a bilateral meeting with External Affairs Minister (EAM) S. Jaishankar, Sikorski spoke of their longstanding relationship, which he said he greatly valued. He did not confirm a separate meeting. The Polish minister also pointed to closer cooperation with Washington. He said he had sat beside US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and exchanged views and ideas about common projects. He declined to disclose the details but said more Polish-American initiatives on the international stage could be expected. On bilateral ties, he said: "I'm glad to say that they're excellent, irrespective of who is in charge, either in Washington or in Warsaw." Sikorski also addressed the difficulty of reaching agreement within the G20. Asked about the prospect of the meeting ending without a joint communiquÃ©, he said he was not surprised, given the wars involving countries represented at the table. "There are countries here represented that don't necessarily see eye to eye, but we need to keep the conversation going." He said the discussions had covered freedom of navigation, energy and food security, issues he described as going back to the G20's roots. The G20 was established in 1999 following the Asian financial crisis. It was elevated to a forum for national leaders in 2008, during the global financial crisis. The African Union became a permanent G20 member at the New Delhi summit in September 2023, during India's presidency.
